sections.title: A tennis court that stopped an army
sections.intro_md:
In April 1944, on a hill in the middle of a small town in the Naga Hills, British and Indian soldiers and the Japanese 31st Division fought for days across a tennis court. The court belonged to the Deputy Commissioner. The Japanese had marched over the mountains from Burma to cut the road to Imphal and, some hoped, open the way to India. They were stopped here. The tennis court is still there, its lines picked out in white concrete, surrounded by 1,420 graves.

In six weeks, on the first day of December, a few kilometres down the road, the state will open the Hornbill Festival: ten days of log drums, war dances, feathered headgear, king chillies and rock bands. That is Nagaland in two scenes. A small hill state of about 20 lakh people, made of more than a dozen peoples who once took each other's heads, who became the most Baptist place on earth, who fought India for independence for decades, and who now invite the world to a party.

sections.title: The state in eight numbers
sections.intro_md:
Nagaland covers **16,579 square km** of hills on India's border with Myanmar, about the size of Kuwait, with Assam to the north and west, Arunachal Pradesh to the north-east and Manipur to the south. Its land rises from 140 m on the Dhansiri river to **3,826 m** at Mount Saramati on the Myanmar border.

Census 2011 counted **19.78 lakh** people. It has 17 districts after a run of new ones: Noklak in 2017, Chümoukedima, Niuland and Tseminyü in 2021, Shamator in 2022 and Meluri in 2024. Kohima is the capital; Dimapur is the largest city. English has been the official language since 1967, but most people talk to each other in Nagamese. Christians are **87.93%**, the highest share of any state, and most are Baptists. It became India's 16th state on 1 December 1963, and Article 371A of the Constitution protects its customary law and land.

sections.title: The land: ridges, a cold valley and a falcon highway
sections.intro_md:
Nagaland is almost all hills, the northern end of the ranges that run down the India-Myanmar border into Myanmar. The Barail range in the south-west, the Japfü range above Kohima and the Patkai and Naga hills to the east rise in long parallel ridges, cut by rivers such as the Doyang, Dikhu, Tizu and Dhansiri.

The hills are wet. Monsoon rain feeds forests of oak, alder, rhododendron and bamboo, and the state flower is the rhododendron and its tree the alder, which Angami and Chakhesang farmers pollard in their fields. Much of the forest has been cut for jhum farming and timber, and wildlife was hunted hard for generations. The turnaround of the past 25 years, led by villages rather than the government, is one of the state's good stories: Khonoma's tragopan sanctuary and Pangti's falcon roost are both community decisions.

spotlights.name: Dzükou Valley

where.label: Behind Mount Japfü, Kohima district and Senapati, Manipur

spotlights.when: About 2,450 m; lilies bloom May to June
spotlights.spot_it: A high, treeless bowl of rolling green hummocks, cut by a winding stream, with no village in sight.
spotlights.story_md: Dzükou sits about 2,450 m up, behind Mount Japfü, on the line between Nagaland and Manipur. From a distance the slopes look like lawn. Up close it is dwarf bamboo, waist high, which is why the valley burns so easily: fires swept it in 2006, 2018, the winter of 2020-21 and again in January 2026, when about 30 stranded trekkers had to be brought out. In May and June a pink lily blooms across the meadows. The usual meaning given for the name is cold water, after the icy stream. Both states claim parts of the valley, and Angami villages on one side and Mao villages on the other each say it is their customary land.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Nagaland's most famous walk, and a live border question.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lawn made of bamboo that keeps catching fire.

spotlights.name: Blyth's tragopan

where.label: Forests of Kohima, Phek and Khonoma

spotlights.spot_it: A pheasant with a rusty red head, bare yellow face and white spots scattered over its back.
spotlights.story_md: The state bird is a shy pheasant almost nobody sees. Males have a red head, yellow facial skin, white spots on the back and two pale blue horns that rise only in courtship. The world population is estimated at 2,500 to 9,999 birds and falling, and the species is listed as vulnerable. In 1998 hunters from Khonoma killed about 300 of them in a single competition. The shock of that number turned the village into a conservation pioneer: its council banned hunting over 20 square km and set up the Khonoma Nature Conservation and Tragopan Sanctuary. The bird is named after Edward Blyth, curator of the Asiatic Society of Bengal's museum in the 19th century.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A state bird that nearly became a hunting trophy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three hundred tragopans in one contest: the day Khonoma changed.

spotlights.name: Mithun

where.label: Across the Naga hills; research centre at Medziphema

spotlights.spot_it: A huge black bovine with white stockings, a flat forehead and thick horns curving out sideways.
spotlights.story_md: The mithun, or gayal, is the state animal, and it is half wild. Owners let it roam the forest and it comes back on its own, though many now fence it in at night because wild dogs take calves. Genetic studies point to the gaur as its maternal ancestor and suggest it was domesticated more than 8,000 years ago near the Assam and Burma border. It is rarely milked or ploughed with. Its job is social: mithun served as currency, paid fines and bride price, and were slaughtered at Feasts of Merit, when a man who had become rich fed the whole village and earned the right to new honours. India's National Research Centre on Mithun is in Medziphema, Nagaland.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Wealth in the Naga hills was counted in mithun, not coins.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cow that is a bank account, and goes for walks on its own.

spotlights.name: Amur falcons at Pangti

where.label: Pangti and the Doyang reservoir, Wokha district

spotlights.spot_it: Clouds of small grey falcons over the Doyang reservoir at dusk, settling on trees and power lines.
spotlights.story_md: Each autumn huge flocks of Amur falcons, small raptors that breed in Siberia and China, stop at the Doyang reservoir in Wokha on their way to southern Africa. In October 2012 a Conservation India team counted nets and spoke to hunters and estimated that 12,000 to 14,000 birds were being caught a day at the peak, perhaps 120,000 to 140,000 a season, mostly to eat and sell. The pictures went round the world. Within weeks the district banned the hunt. Pangti, a Lotha village, then did something rarer: it turned protection into its own project, with village patrols and homestays. The 2013 and 2014 seasons recorded no killing at Doyang, and Pangti now calls itself the falcon capital of the world.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the fastest conservation turnarounds anywhere in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: From 14,000 a day to zero in a year.

spotlights.name: Great hornbill
spotlights.when: Gives the Hornbill Festival its name
spotlights.spot_it: A large black and white bird with a huge yellow bill topped by a hollow casque.
spotlights.story_md: The Hornbill Festival is named after this bird because nearly every Naga people uses it in folklore and dress. Its long black and white tail feathers crown warrior headgear, and carved hornbill heads decorate morungs and gateposts, including the gate at Kisama. Wearing hornbill feathers was a mark of rank, often earned in war or by giving feasts. The bird needs large old trees with hollows to nest in: the female seals herself inside with mud and the male feeds her through a slit for weeks. That makes it a good gauge of old forest, and hunting and logging have made it rare in much of the state. Many dancers now wear imitation feathers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state's biggest party is named after a bird most Nagas rarely see.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bird that walls itself in, and a festival that throws its doors open.

sections.title: People by numbers
sections.intro_md:
Census 2011 counted **1,978,502** people, about 0.16% of India. That makes Nagaland one of the smallest states by population. It is also the only state whose population fell between 2001 and 2011, from 1,990,036, a drop of about 0.6%. The likeliest explanation is that earlier counts had been inflated, and 2011 corrected them, so the decline is partly a statistical effect.

Density is **119 people per square km**, less than a third of India's. Over 71% live in villages. The sex ratio, 931 women per 1,000 men, is below India's 943, partly because of male migrants in Dimapur. Literacy was **79.55%** in 2011, above India's 73%, and the state reports far higher figures today. Almost everyone born in Nagaland belongs to a Scheduled Tribe, and the Naga peoples, together with the Kuki and Kachari, make up the large majority.

sections.title: Seventeen peoples, one name
sections.intro_md:
Naga is not one people but a family of them. The word itself was an outsider's label, of doubtful origin; one Assamese explanation links it to people with pierced ears. Across India and Myanmar, 89 groups were classified as Naga by 2015, speaking more than 89 languages and dialects, most unintelligible to each other. Inside Nagaland the state recognises 17 major tribes: Angami, Ao, Chakhesang, Chang, Khiamniungan, Konyak, Kuki, Kachari, Lotha, Phom, Pochury, Rengma, Sangtam, Sümi, Tikhir, Yimkhiung and Zeliang.

Each has its own district heartland, language, dress, festival and history. Under British rule each village was mostly self-governing, and there was no shared Naga identity. That came later, built by war, by the church, by the common language Nagamese, and by the national movement. Today a Naga will usually tell you their tribe first and their village second, and Naga third.

spotlights.name: Konyak

where.label: Mon district, the land of the Anghs

spotlights.spot_it: Elders with blue-black tattoos across the face, brass head pendants, and caps with boar tusks and horns.
spotlights.story_md: The Konyak are the largest Naga people, with 237,568 in Nagaland in 2011, most of them in Mon district. Their villages were ruled by hereditary chiefs called Anghs, and some still are. A Konyak man earned his facial tattoo by taking an enemy's head, and heads were kept as trophies in the village men's house. The Konyak were also the last Naga group to accept Christianity, which is why the last tattooed headhunters, now very old men, are Konyak. They are skilled smiths: Konyak villages made guns, gunpowder, machetes and brass. Their language is closer to Garo and Bodo than to most other Naga languages. Their great festival is Aoleang, from 1 to 6 April.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Most of the images people outside have of Nagaland come from here.
spotlights.memory_hook: The last tattooed headhunters are grandfathers who go to church.

spotlights.name: Angami
spotlights.when: Southern Nagaland; festival Sekrenyi in February
spotlights.spot_it: Black shawls with bands of red and yellow, feathered headgear, and terraced rice fields stepping down every hillside.
spotlights.story_md: The Angami live around Kohima and are the people of Khonoma, Kohima village and Jakhama. They are known for wet rice grown on terraces cut into steep slopes and watered by channels, a rarity in hills where most people farm by slash and burn. Angami villages resisted the British longer than almost anyone: Khonoma fought until a peace in March 1880. Angami Zapu Phizo, who led the Naga national movement, was born in Khonoma. Many Angami died in the Battle of Kohima in 1944, which was fought through their town. Their most important festival is Sekrenyi, a ten-day purification in February. The Lohe shawl, with embroidered animals, is theirs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The capital, the war and the national movement all run through Angami country.
spotlights.memory_hook: Terraces, rebellion and Kohima: the Angami trinity.

spotlights.name: Ao
spotlights.spot_it: Women in dark skirts with coloured bands, men in red shawls, and a reputation for schools and pulpits.
spotlights.story_md: The Ao live mostly in Mokokchung district and number about 227,000. They call themselves Aoer, those who came, meaning across the Dikhu river. The Ao were the first Naga people to become Christian: Edward Winter Clark, an American Baptist, reached the Ao village of Molungkimong in 1872 and his mission put the Ao language into writing. That head start shows. Ao families produced many of Nagaland's first teachers, doctors, pastors and civil servants, including Talimeren Ao, India's first Olympic football captain. Their festivals are Moatsü in the first week of May, after sowing, and Tsüngremong in August, at harvest. Ao speech has several varieties, the main ones being Chungli and Mongsen.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Ao were Nagaland's gateway to literacy and the church.
spotlights.memory_hook: First to the Bible, first to the classroom.

spotlights.name: Sümi
spotlights.spot_it: Tall headgear with hornbill feathers and beads, warrior spears, and a kicking fight called aki kiti.
spotlights.story_md: The Sümi, once spelled Sema, are centred on Zunheboto in central Nagaland and have spread widely across the state. They gave Naga cooking one of its signature tastes: axone, the fermented soybean whose name in Sümi means deep smell. They also gave Naga sport aki kiti, a combat game in which two men try to kick each other off balance using only the soles of their feet. Their feasts are Tuluni in July and Ahuna in November, the harvest festival at which new rice is cooked in bamboo tubes. Sümi headgear, tall and crowned with feathers, is among the most photographed at Hornbill.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A people whose food and sport have spread far beyond their district.
spotlights.memory_hook: The tribe that taught Nagaland to love a smell.

spotlights.name: Chakhesang
spotlights.spot_it: White shawls with black bands, and some of the best polyphonic folk singing in the hills.
spotlights.story_md: Chakhesang is a made name. It joins the first syllables of three groups, the Chokri, the Khezha and the Sangtam, who separated from the larger Angami and Sangtam identities in the 1940s. They live mainly in Phek district, in the southeast, where rice terraces cover the hillsides around Pfutsero, one of the coldest towns in the state. The Chokri share a body of folk song called li: the Tetseo Sisters, the state's best known folk group, sing in Chokri and draw on a traditional songbook of 223 common songs plus many more passed down by ear. Chakhesang villages also have a strong tradition of terrace farming and of growing rice without chemical inputs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that Naga tribal names are living, recent and negotiated.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three names welded into one: CHOK-KHE-SANG.

sections.title: Before the British: village states and a plains kingdom
sections.intro_md:
For most of their history the Naga hills had no single ruler. Each village was a small fortified state on a hilltop, with its own council, its own fields and its own enemies. Villages raided each other for heads, made alliances, and traded salt, cotton, iron and cloth with the plains. Several Naga peoples share a story of origin at Makhel, in the hills now in Manipur.

On the plain at the foot of the hills stood the Dimasa Kachari kingdom, whose capital at Dimapur left brick ruins that still puzzle archaeologists. To the north the Ahom kings of Assam dealt with Naga villages through trade, tribute and war. The British arrived after taking Assam in 1826. They sent expeditions into the hills from the 1830s, set up a district at Kohima in 1878, and fought their last serious Naga war at Khonoma in 1879-80. From 1872 American Baptist missionaries worked in the Ao hills, and within a century the hills were Christian.

spotlights.name: Kachari Rajbari ruins
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of brick pillars 3 to 4 m high, each topped with a rounded dome like a mushroom.
spotlights.story_md: In the middle of Dimapur, Nagaland's busiest town, stand rows of strange brick pillars with domed tops. They are the remains of the capital of the Dimasa Kachari kingdom, which ruled the plains below the Naga hills for centuries. A British officer, Godwin-Austen, measured them in 1874 at about 12 to 13 feet, the tallest near 15, and noted lotus carvings. Nobody knows what they were for. One local belief says they were pieces for a giant board game. The Ahom chronicles describe an Ahom attack on the city in the 1520s, after which the Kacharis moved their capital south. The site is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India but poorly kept.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that the plains edge of Nagaland was once a royal city, not a frontier.
spotlights.memory_hook: Stone mushrooms in a busy town, and no one knows why.

spotlights.name: Headhunting and the head trophy

where.label: Across the Naga hills, longest among the Konyak

spotlights.spot_it: Carved wooden heads on baskets, brass pendants shaped like rows of tiny faces, tattoos on chests and cheeks.
spotlights.story_md: For centuries many Naga villages raided each other for heads. A head brought the spirit and fertility of the dead into the taker's village, and it was the passage into manhood: among the Konyak only a man who had taken a head could wear the facial tattoo. Heads were kept in the morung or the men's house, and status objects echoed them, like the Konyak basket here with two carved heads, and brass pendants in which each small face recorded a kill. British officers tried to end the practice in the 19th century, and Christian conversion did most of the work in the 20th. It is a history Nagas now discuss openly, without either shame or romance.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shaped Naga villages, from their hilltop sites to their art.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every little brass face on the pendant was once a person.

spotlights.name: Khonoma
spotlights.spot_it: A fortified Angami hill village above terraced paddy, with stone gateways and memorial stones.
spotlights.story_md: Khonoma fought the British longer than any Naga village. In October 1879 its warriors ambushed and killed the political officer Guybon Damant and 27 others, and the British needed a four-month siege before a peace on 27 March 1880, the last organised Naga resistance. Phizo was born here in 1904. The village made news again in 1998 for the opposite reason: villagers killed about 300 Blyth's tragopans in a hunting contest. The council responded with a hunting ban over 20 square km and a community sanctuary, and in 2005 Khonoma was called India's first green village. Its 2011 population was 1,943, and its literacy rate, 83.4%, beat the state's.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One village holds the story of Naga resistance and Naga conservation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Khonoma: last to surrender, first to go green.

sections.title: Kohima, 1944: the battle that saved India's north-east
sections.intro_md:
In March 1944 Japan launched Operation U-Go, an invasion of India from Burma aimed at Imphal and Kohima. The Japanese 31st Division under Lieutenant General Kōtoku Satō crossed the hills and on 4 April reached Kohima, a small hill station that guarded the road from the railway at Dimapur to Imphal. The siege began on 6 April. A scratch garrison held a ridge for two weeks, fighting at times across the Deputy Commissioner's tennis court, until the British 2nd Division broke through on 18 April. Fighting went on until 22 June.

British and Indian losses at Kohima were 4,064. Japanese battle casualties were at least 5,764, and thousands more died of starvation and disease on the retreat. Soldiers of the Indian National Army fought on the Japanese side. Naga villagers carried loads, guided patrols, hid wounded men, and paid heavily as their villages were fought over. Historians have called Kohima and Imphal the Stalingrad of the East.

spotlights.name: The Battle of the Tennis Court
spotlights.spot_it: White concrete lines marking a tennis court among the graves on Garrison Hill.
spotlights.story_md: In April 1944 the Japanese 31st Division came over the hills from Burma to take Kohima and cut the road to Imphal. About 2,500 men, a thousand of them non-combatants, held a ridge in the town under Colonel Hugh Richards. On one slope was the Deputy Commissioner's bungalow and his tennis court. For days the two sides fought across the court, close enough to throw grenades over the net line. By the time the British 2nd Division broke through on 18 April, the defenders held a perimeter about 350 m square. Fighting went on until June. The court is still there, its lines painted white in concrete, inside the war cemetery.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Japanese advance into India stopped here.
spotlights.memory_hook: The most dangerous tennis court in history had no net.

spotlights.name: The Kohima Epitaph
spotlights.spot_it: A plain stone with four short lines: When you go home, tell them of us and say...
spotlights.story_md: The memorial to the British 2nd Division carries the lines: When you go home, tell them of us and say, for your tomorrow, we gave our today. They are attributed to the classical scholar John Maxwell Edmonds, who probably had in mind the Greek epitaph for the Spartans at Thermopylae. The words have travelled far beyond Kohima. They are read at Remembrance services across Britain and the Commonwealth, carved on stones in English towns, and quoted at Indian Army memorials. A cherry tree beside the tennis court carries the second half on a brass plaque. The original tree was shot to pieces in the battle, which is why some call it the battle under the cherry tree.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Perhaps the most quoted war memorial words in English.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four lines, written for Thermopylae, finished at Kohima.

spotlights.name: Memorial to the cremated
spotlights.spot_it: A long stone wall of names at the top of the terraces, not a field of graves.
spotlights.story_md: Kohima War Cemetery holds 1,420 Commonwealth burials. It also remembers 917 Hindu and Sikh soldiers who were cremated according to their faith and so have no graves; their names are carved on a memorial at the top of the hill. The army that held Kohima was largely Indian: Assam Regiment, Assam Rifles, Rajputs, Punjabis and many more, with Naga villagers carrying supplies and wounded and guiding patrols. On the other side were not only Japanese troops but also soldiers of Subhas Chandra Bose's Indian National Army, who hoped to march on Delhi. So Indians fought on both sides at Kohima, which is part of why the battle is remembered so differently in Britain, Japan and India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A reminder that this was an Indian battle as much as a British one.
spotlights.memory_hook: 917 names and no graves: the soldiers who went to fire, not earth.

spotlights.name: Charles Pawsey
spotlights.when: 1894 to 1972; Deputy Commissioner of the Naga Hills
spotlights.spot_it: The British civil officer whose house and tennis court became the front line.
spotlights.story_md: Charles Pawsey was the Deputy Commissioner of the Naga Hills in 1944, the senior civil officer in Kohima. It was his bungalow above the tennis court that the Japanese and British fought over, and he refused to leave during the siege. His standing with Naga village leaders mattered: Naga porters, scouts and guides worked for the British side through the campaign, and Naga villages fed and hid soldiers. After the war Pawsey stayed on into the transition and dealt with the first Naga political demands. The photograph here shows him much younger, as a soldier in the First World War, in which he had served before joining the Indian Civil Service.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His house is now a cemetery, and his trust with Naga elders helped win the battle.
spotlights.memory_hook: A civil servant who would not leave his own lawn.

spotlights.name: Kōtoku Satō
spotlights.spot_it: The Japanese general who disobeyed orders and walked his starving division out of Kohima.
spotlights.story_md: Lieutenant General Kōtoku Satō led the 31st Division across the Chindwin and the hills to Kohima. He had warned his superiors that the plan relied on capturing British supplies that might never be captured, and that is what happened. By late May his men were starving and sick. Satō pulled them back without permission, one of the very few times a Japanese divisional commander openly defied orders in the war. He was removed in early July. Japanese battle casualties around Kohima were at least 5,764, and many more died of hunger and disease on the retreat. Japanese donors later paid for most of Kohima's Catholic cathedral as a memorial to their dead.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His retreat turned a defeat into the collapse of the whole offensive.
spotlights.memory_hook: A general who chose his men over his orders.

sections.title: From the Naga Club to the 16th state
sections.intro_md:
Naga politics began with men who had seen the wider world. Nagas who served in France in the British labour corps in the First World War formed the **Naga Club** in 1918, and in 1929 it told the Simon Commission that the Nagas wished to be left alone to decide their own future. The Naga National Council followed in 1946. Under Angami Zapu Phizo it demanded full independence, declared it on 14 August 1947, and in 1951 held a plebiscite that it said showed 99.9% support.

India refused, and from 1956 the hills were at war, with an underground Naga government on one side and the Army on the other. Moderates negotiated statehood, which came on 1 December 1963. The fight went on: the Shillong Accord of 1975 split the movement, the NSCN was founded in 1980 and itself split in 1988, a ceasefire with the NSCN (IM) has held since 1997, and a Framework Agreement was signed on 3 August 2015. Its text has never been made public, and a final settlement is still awaited.

spotlights.name: Angami Zapu Phizo
spotlights.spot_it: The father of Naga nationalism, who declared independence a day before India did.
spotlights.story_md: Phizo was born in Khonoma on 16 May 1904. He became president of the Naga National Council in 1949, by one vote, and turned it toward full independence. On 14 August 1947 he sent a telegram declaring the Nagas independent. On 16 May 1951 the NNC held a plebiscite and claimed 99.9% support for independence; India rejected the vote. In 1956 he formed an underground Naga government and the hills went to war. He escaped through East Pakistan and reached London in June 1960, where he lived in exile for 30 years and was never given a visa home. He died in Bromley on 30 April 1990, and his body was flown back to Kohima for burial.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every Naga political debate still argues with his legacy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thirty years in a London suburb, buried in Kohima.

spotlights.name: Rani Gaidinliu
spotlights.spot_it: A Zeliangrong teenager who led a revolt against the British and spent 14 years in jail.
spotlights.story_md: Gaidinliu was 13 when she joined the Heraka movement of her cousin Haipou Jadonang, who preached a reformed Naga faith and resistance to British rule. After the British hanged Jadonang in 1931, she took over at 16, told her people to stop paying taxes, and was captured in 1932 and given a life sentence. Jawaharlal Nehru met her in prison in 1937 and called her Rani, queen. She was freed in 1947. Later she opposed both Christian conversion and the Naga underground, which made her a hero to the Indian state and a divisive figure among many Christian Nagas. She received the Padma Bhushan in 1982 and died in 1993.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Her life shows that Naga history is not one story but several.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nehru named her queen; her own people still argue about her.

spotlights.name: Statehood, 1 December 1963
spotlights.spot_it: The anniversary that the Hornbill Festival opens on every year: 1 December.
spotlights.story_md: Nagaland became India's 16th state on 1 December 1963, the result of the 16-point agreement that moderate Naga leaders of the Naga People's Convention signed with Delhi in 1960. It was tiny, with fewer than four lakh people, and it was created while the war with the underground was still on. Its price was Article 371A, added to the Constitution in 1962: no Act of Parliament on Naga religious or social practices, customary law, justice under customary law, or the ownership and transfer of land applies unless the state assembly agrees. That is why most land in Nagaland is owned by villages, clans and families, not the state. The Hornbill Festival opens on statehood day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Article 371A makes Nagaland one of the most self-governing states in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Statehood day and festival day are the same day.

sections.title: Many languages, one market tongue
sections.intro_md:
Nagaland may be the most multilingual place of its size in India. Each Naga people has its own language, and many have several dialects: Ao has Chungli and Mongsen, the Chakhesang speak Chokri and Khezha. Most belong to the Tibeto-Burman family, but they are often as different from each other as Spanish from German. Konyak, for example, is closer to Garo and Bodo than to Angami.

The state made **English** its official language in 1967, partly so that no tribe's language would be ranked above the others, and schools teach in English from early on. In daily life, though, the common language is Nagamese, an Assamese-based creole born in the barter markets of the plains. Missionaries put many Naga languages into Roman script and translated the Bible into them, so a Naga village's first book was usually scripture. Several languages are now taught in school as subjects, and young Nagas often speak three or four.

spotlights.name: Nagamese

where.label: Spoken statewide; born in the Assam plains markets

spotlights.spot_it: Assamese-sounding words with a simple grammar, heard in every bus, market and office in the state.
spotlights.story_md: Nagaland has more than a dozen major languages and many dialects, often unintelligible from one valley to the next. The Ao in Mokokchung cannot simply chat with the Angami in Kohima in their own tongues. The bridge is Nagamese, a creole built mostly on Assamese words that grew up in the barter markets where hill people traded with Assamese merchants. Ethnologue counts about 30,000 first-language speakers, mostly in Dimapur, and hundreds of thousands who use it as a second language. Few people are fluent in English, the official language since 1967, so politicians, preachers, nurses and radio hosts use Nagamese. It is the true common language of a state that has no common mother tongue.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The everyday glue of Naga public life is a language no one officially chose.
spotlights.memory_hook: A market tongue that became a state's real language.

sections.title: The most Baptist place on earth
sections.intro_md:
In 1872 there were no Christians in the Naga hills. By 2011, **87.93%** of Nagaland's people were Christian, the highest share of any Indian state, and about three in four Nagas belong to Baptist churches, which is why Nagaland is often called the only predominantly Baptist state in the world. The change came through American Baptist missionaries working from Assam, then through Naga evangelists who carried the faith village to village, and fastest of all during the war years after 1950.

Church is the centre of Naga social life. Village churches are often the largest buildings, and Christmas is the biggest festival of the year. The old religion did not vanish entirely: Heraka survives among the Zeliangrong, and many old festivals are now kept with prayers in place of sacrifices. Hindus, at 8.75% mostly migrants and plains communities, and Muslims, at 2.47%, are small minorities.

spotlights.name: Edward Winter Clark
spotlights.spot_it: An American Baptist from New York who wrote down the Ao language and started the Naga church.
spotlights.story_md: Edward Winter Clark, a Baptist minister from New York, worked from Assam before going up into the Ao hills. Fifteen converts were baptised at Molungkimong in 1872, and Clark moved there in 1876 to live among them; it is remembered as the first Christian village in Nagaland. With his wife Mary he turned spoken Ao into writing and compiled the first Ao dictionary, and he started the first school in the hills. In 1894 the mission moved its centre to Impur. A century later Christians are about 88% of Nagaland and Baptists the largest church. That transformation ended headhunting, but it also cost many older practices, songs and festivals, a loss many Nagas now work to recover.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One missionary's village began the change that defines modern Nagaland.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifteen baptisms in 1872, a Baptist state a century later.

spotlights.name: Mary Help of Christians Cathedral
spotlights.spot_it: A huge church whose front is shaped like the gable of a Naga house, high on a Kohima hill.
spotlights.story_md: Kohima's Catholic cathedral was begun in 1986 and consecrated in January 1991. Its façade copies the front of a traditional Naga house, with a steep gable, so it looks as if it grew from the hill. Inside hangs a carved wooden crucifix about 16 feet tall, one of the largest in Asia. Most of the roughly three crore rupees it cost came from Japanese donors who wanted a memorial to the Japanese soldiers who died at Kohima in 1944, and the cathedral has hosted reconciliation meetings between British and Japanese veterans. It holds about 4,500 people. Catholics are a minority in Nagaland, but this is the state's best known church building.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A church that doubles as a peace memorial between old enemies.
spotlights.memory_hook: Japanese money, a Naga roof and a 16-foot Christ.

sections.title: Drums, songs and the warrior dance
sections.intro_md:
Naga music was made for the village, not the concert hall. Songs went with every task: clearing fields, carrying wood, mourning, courting, going to war. Many peoples sing in parts that interlock, and some, like the Chokri Chakhesang, have hundreds of traditional songs. Instruments are simple and made from the forest: bamboo flutes and mouth organs, horns from mithun, a one-string fiddle called tati, and above all the log drum, a whole hollowed tree.

Dance is collective. Men dance war dances in lines with spears and shields; women dance slower, sung dances of harvest and welcome. Missionaries discouraged much of this as pagan, and for decades many young Nagas preferred hymns and, later, rock music: Kohima has one of India's oldest rock scenes. In the last 25 years the Hornbill Festival and groups like the Tetseo Sisters have made the old songs and dances fashionable again.

spotlights.name: The log drum

where.label: Every Naga village; most famous among the Konyak, Ao, Chang and Phom

spotlights.spot_it: A whole tree trunk, hollowed and carved into a long boat shape, beaten by a row of men with heavy sticks.
spotlights.story_md: The log drum is a hollowed tree, sometimes over 10 m long, often carved at one end into a buffalo or hornbill head, and kept in its own shed. Making one is a village event: the tree is felled, shaped in the forest, then dragged home by dozens of men in a ritual procession, as the Chang do in the Hornbill arena. Beaten by a line of men with pestle-like sticks, it could signal a raid, a death, a festival or a call to assembly across valleys. The Ao call it süngkong, which roughly means crowing wood. Many log drums have been lost or have rotted, and making a new one is now rare and celebrated.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Before phones, this was the village's alarm, radio and heartbeat.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tree that crows across the valley.

spotlights.name: The Naga warrior dance

where.label: Kisama and village festivals across the state

spotlights.spot_it: Lines of men in shawls and feathered headgear, spears and shields raised, stamping, chanting and leaping.
spotlights.story_md: Every Naga people has war dances, and each is distinct in step, chant and costume, but they share a grammar: men in a tight line or circle, spears and dao held up, a call and a roar, sudden leaps and mock charges. Women's dances, which are often slower and sung, celebrate harvest and courtship. The dances once prepared men for raids and celebrated their return. Today they are performed at Sekrenyi, Moatsü, Aoleang and above all at the Hornbill Festival, where each tribe has its own morung and performs in the central arena. To an outside eye they look alike. To Nagas, the step and the headgear say exactly which people and often which village a dancer is from.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The dances are how each Naga people shows itself to the others.
spotlights.memory_hook: A spear in the air, and everybody knows which village you are from.

spotlights.name: The Tetseo Sisters and li
spotlights.spot_it: Four sisters in Chakhesang dress singing close, interlocking harmonies, one plucking a one-string tati.
spotlights.story_md: Mütsevelü, Azine, Kuvelü and Alüne Tetseo grew up in Kohima singing li, the folk songs of the Chokri Chakhesang. Li are sung for work, love, children, war and grief, often in interlocking parts. The Chakhesang have a traditional songbook of 223 common songs and many more passed down by ear. The sisters sing in Chokri, sometimes with the one-stringed tati or a mithun horn, and have mixed the old songs with pop, including covers and originals. Their first album, Li Chapter One, came out in 2011 and the EP A Slice of Li in 2019. They have performed for Nagaland in Thailand, Myanmar, China, South Korea, the UK and the US.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They made tribal folk song cool for young Nagas again.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four sisters, one string, 223 songs.

sections.title: Shawls, beads, brass and ink
sections.intro_md:
Naga craft is wearable. A Naga in full dress carries a family history: a shawl whose bands name the tribe and the wearer's rank, a headdress of cane and hornbill feathers, necklaces of carnelian, glass and shell, armlets of ivory or brass, and among the Konyak a brass pendant of tiny heads. Every piece once had to be earned through war or feasting, and wearing what you had not earned was an insult.

Women weave on back-strap looms at home, and weaving is still common in villages. Men work cane, bamboo, wood and metal. Konyak villages were famous for smithing and carving. Some crafts have been commercialised for the tourist market and for the many Nagas who wear traditional dress to weddings, church and the assembly. The state's handloom and craft stalls at Kisama are among the busiest parts of the Hornbill Festival.

spotlights.name: Naga shawls

where.label: Woven in villages across the state

spotlights.when: Back-strap loom; patterns by tribe and rank
spotlights.spot_it: Thick cotton shawls, usually black or dark blue, with bold bands of red, white and yellow; each tribe's bands are different.
spotlights.story_md: Naga women weave on back-strap looms, with one end tied to a post and the other to a strap round the weaver's waist, so the body itself keeps the warp tight. A shawl is an identity card. Its colours and bands say which people the wearer belongs to and, traditionally, what rank he had earned. Some designs were reserved for warriors who had taken heads or men who had given Feasts of Merit: the Ao Tsüngkotepsü carries a central white band painted with mithun, tigers, spears and human heads. The Angami Lohe shawl has embroidered animals. Wearing another man's honour shawl was once an insult. Today the shawls are worn to church, weddings and assembly sessions.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Cloth carries rank, clan and history in a society that did not write.
spotlights.memory_hook: Read the stripes and you can read the man.

spotlights.name: Naga beads
spotlights.spot_it: Heavy, many-strand necklaces of orange-red carnelian, yellow and blue glass, white shell and brass.
spotlights.story_md: Naga jewellery is heavy and bold. Men and women wear necklaces of many strands: orange carnelian, coloured glass, conch shell discs, brass bells, boar tusks and, in old pieces, cowries. None of the shell or carnelian is local. Conch came from the coast and carnelian and glass travelled up through Assam and Burma, which means the hills, long described as isolated, were in fact tied into trade routes across the region. Beads were wealth that could be worn, inherited and given at marriages. Antique Naga necklaces are now prized by collectors abroad, and families who still own them keep them for festivals and weddings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Beads prove the Naga hills were never cut off from the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seashells, a thousand kilometres from the sea.

spotlights.name: Konyak facial tattoos
spotlights.when: Last given in the mid-20th century
spotlights.spot_it: Dark blue-black lines across the face, chest and arms of very old Konyak men.
spotlights.story_md: Among the Konyak, the facial tattoo was earned. A young man who had taken a head in a raid had his face tattooed, and chest and arm tattoos marked further status. Women had their own tattoos on legs and arms at marriage. The work was done by women with thorns and soot. When Christianity and the government ended raiding, the tattoos stopped too, so the men who carry them are now in their eighties and nineties, and photographers come from around the world to meet them in villages like Longwa. Many of these men are devout Christians and speak of their youth with a mix of pride and distance. When they are gone, the living practice goes with them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The last living link to the headhunting era is written on these faces.
spotlights.memory_hook: A face that was a trophy case.

spotlights.name: Feathered headgear

where.label: Worn at festivals across the state

spotlights.when: Hornbill feathers, bear fur, cane and boar tusks
spotlights.spot_it: Woven cane helmets crowned with hornbill feathers, rimmed with fur, tusks or horns, and tied with bright yarn.
spotlights.story_md: Naga headgear is architecture for the head. The base is woven cane or bamboo. Onto it go hornbill tail feathers, which once had to be earned, red-dyed goat hair, bear fur, boar tusks, mithun horns, beads and coloured yarn. The shapes differ sharply between peoples: tall fanned feathers among the Sümi, horned caps among the Konyak, a halo of feathers among the Angami. Each part could signal deeds in war or the feasts a man had given. Because real hornbill feathers are now protected and scarce, many headdresses at Hornbill use substitutes. A good headdress is still an heirloom, worn by father and son, and it is often the first thing a visitor notices.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Headgear tells you tribe, status and family at a glance.
spotlights.memory_hook: A crown you had to earn, feather by feather.

sections.title: Smoke, ferment and fire
sections.intro_md:
Naga food is built on rice, pork, greens and chilli, with almost no oil, very little dry spice and no dairy. Its flavours come from three things. Smoke: meat and fish dried for weeks over the kitchen fire. Fermentation: bamboo shoot, soybean (axone), fish and even yam leaves left to sour and deepen. Fire: the Naga king chilli, one of the hottest in the world.

A typical meal is a heap of rice, a boiled vegetable or broth, a meat dish such as smoked pork with bamboo shoot, and a sharp chutney. Pork is the favourite meat. Beef, chicken, fish, snails, and in season silkworm pupae, hornet larvae and weaver ants are all eaten. Rice beer, called zutho by the Angami, is the traditional drink, though alcohol has been officially banned since 1989. Many mainland Indians find Naga food startling. Naga cooks find mainland food oily and heavy.

spotlights.name: Raja mircha, the Naga king chilli
spotlights.spot_it: A wrinkled, thin-skinned chilli, red or orange when ripe, about 6 to 8 cm long, with a heat that builds.
spotlights.story_md: The Naga king chilli, also called bhut jolokia or ghost pepper, measures around a million Scoville units, roughly 200 times hotter than Tabasco. Guinness World Records named it the world's hottest chilli in 2007; it has since been overtaken by bred varieties such as the Carolina Reaper. Naga mircha received a Geographical Indication tag on 2 December 2008. Nagas use it fresh, dried, smoked and pickled, often with pork or fermented fish. Its other careers: farmers smear it on fences to keep wild elephants away, and India's defence research organisation proposed chilli grenades for crowd control in 2009. Its burn builds slowly, so first-timers often take a second bite before they realise.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most famous ingredient from the hills, and a world-record holder.
spotlights.memory_hook: A ghost on the tongue: it waits, then it haunts.

spotlights.name: Smoked pork with bamboo shoot
spotlights.spot_it: Dark, almost black chunks of pork, cooked down with sour bamboo shoot, chilli and sometimes axone.
spotlights.story_md: Pork is the meat of Nagaland, and the classic way to eat it is smoked. Strips of fatty pork hang for days on the rack above the kitchen fire until they are dark, firm and smoky. They are then cooked with fermented bamboo shoot, which gives a sharp sourness, plus king chilli, ginger, garlic and, for many families, axone. The dish is not oily or creamy: Naga cooking uses little oil and few dry spices, relying on smoke, fermentation and chilli instead. It is eaten with plenty of rice and boiled greens. Smoked pork is at every celebration from Christmas to a wedding, and Naga students in Delhi and Bengaluru carry it home in their luggage.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the dish that tastes most of a Naga kitchen.
spotlights.memory_hook: Smoke, sour and fire: the Naga trinity.

spotlights.name: Axone, fermented soybean

where.label: Sümi country, Zunheboto, and across the state

spotlights.when: Made at home over several days
spotlights.spot_it: A brown paste or cake of fermented soybeans wrapped in leaves, with a powerful smell.
spotlights.story_md: Axone is the Sümi word for deep smell, and it lives up to it. Soybeans are boiled until soft, left to ferment for three or four days in summer or about a week in winter, crushed in a wooden mortar and wrapped in banana leaf parcels, sometimes dried by the fire. Fermentation breaks down protein into a deep savoury flavour, like a hill cousin of miso or natto. It is how a hill diet with little dairy gets protein and umami. Cooks add it to pork, snails and chutneys. The smell is so strong that the 2019 film Axone is built around a group of northeastern friends in Delhi trying to cook it without angering the neighbours.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A food that sits at the centre of Naga identity in other Indian cities.
spotlights.memory_hook: The smell that got its own film.

sections.title: The land of festivals
sections.intro_md:
Nagaland calls itself the land of festivals, and every people has at least two: one tied to sowing, one to harvest. They follow the farming year, so dates shift by village, but the main ones are now fixed. Sekrenyi for the Angami in February, Aoleang for the Konyak in April, Moatsü for the Ao in May, Tuluni for the Sümi in July, Tsüngremong for the Ao in August, Tokhü Emong for the Lotha and Ngada for the Rengma in November, and Ahuna for the Sümi too.

In most of them, work in the fields stops, rice beer is brewed, animals are slaughtered and shared, and young people sing and dance. Christianity changed them: sacrifices and some rites dropped away and prayers came in. Then in 2000 the state created a festival for everyone, the Hornbill, which now draws visitors from across India and abroad each December. Christmas, though not a tribal festival, is the biggest celebration of all.

spotlights.name: Hornbill Festival

where.label: Kisama Heritage Village, 12 km south of Kohima

spotlights.spot_it: Ten days of every Naga people at once: morungs in a row, dances in an arena, log drums, wrestling, chilli eating and rock bands.
spotlights.story_md: The state government started the Hornbill Festival in December 2000 to bring all the Naga peoples together in one place and to draw tourists. It runs from 1 to 10 December, starting on statehood day, at Kisama Heritage Village, where each tribe has built its own morung. Days are for dances, songs, games, crafts and food stalls; evenings bring the Hornbill International Rock Festival in Kohima, because Nagaland has one of India's oldest rock scenes. There is Naga wrestling, archery and a king chilli eating contest. Nagas call it the festival of festivals. Critics say it turns living culture into a show, but it has also helped revive dances and crafts that were fading.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made Nagaland a destination and every tribe a host.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seventeen peoples, one village, ten days.

spotlights.name: Sekrenyi
spotlights.spot_it: Young Angami men bathing at the village well at dawn, then days of songs, feasts and a new boundary gate.
spotlights.story_md: Sekrenyi is the Angami festival of purification. Its name joins sekre, sanctification, and nyi, festival. It begins on the 25th day of the Angami month Kezei, usually 25 February. On the first day the village well is cleaned and holy water sprinkled. On the second, young men bathe at the well and a cock is sacrificed: how it falls is read as an omen. The fourth day is the Angami new year, with three days of feasting and song. Later comes a hunt and the replacing of a boundary gate. No field work is done during the festival, and after it farming, building and marriages can begin. Christian villages keep a shorter five-day version without the rituals.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It marks the Angami year and the passage of boys into men.
spotlights.memory_hook: Wash at the well, and the year starts clean.

spotlights.name: Aoleang
spotlights.spot_it: Konyak men and women in long lines, chanting and stepping, with log drums beating through the night.
spotlights.story_md: Aoleang is the Konyak new year and spring festival, held from 1 to 6 April. It closes the old year and opens the season of sowing, and it blesses land and seed before planting. Each day has its own task: preparing food and rice beer, feasting, dancing, and visiting relatives and friends. The great log drums are beaten, and men and women dance in long lines in full dress, including some of the last tattooed elders. In Christian villages, prayers are now said in church as part of it. Aoleang is the best time to see Mon district at its most alive, though the roads in April can be slow and the permits must be in order.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Konyak year turns here.
spotlights.memory_hook: April in Mon: drums, dances and the last tattooed elders.

sections.title: How people live: villages that govern themselves
sections.intro_md:
The basic unit of Naga life is still the village, and the village is still powerful. Under Article 371A most land belongs to villages, clans and families, so the state cannot simply acquire it. Village councils run customary courts, manage forests and decide who may hunt. Clans matter: you marry outside your clan, and your clan stands behind you in disputes.

The church sets much of the moral tone. Alcohol has been banned since 1989, though bootleg liquor is easy to find. A 2020 ban on dog meat was struck down by the High Court in 2023, which described it as an accepted food in Nagaland. Outsiders need an Inner Line Permit to enter, a rule dating from 1873 that protects land and jobs. Women run much of the economy, from markets to NGOs, but customary bodies are male and women's political representation came late. Two tensions run through modern Naga life: customary law against individual rights, and tribe against the wider Naga identity.

spotlights.name: The morung
spotlights.spot_it: A large house with carved front posts, often with buffalo horns or hornbill motifs, at the edge of a village.
spotlights.story_md: The morung was the school, barracks and club of a Naga village. Boys moved in when they reached a certain age and stayed until they married. There they learned the clan's history, songs, crafts, farming and the techniques of war, guarded the village at night and worked in teams for the community. Girls had their own dormitories in many groups. The Angami call it kichuki, the Ao ariju. Carvings on the posts showed hornbills, tigers, mithun and warriors, and some held the log drum and heads. Schools and churches emptied most morungs during the 20th century. The idea survives in name: Naga organisations, magazines and even Nagaland's best known newspaper, The Morung Express, use it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the institution that made a Naga boy into a villager and a warrior.
spotlights.memory_hook: A village's boarding school with spears.

spotlights.name: The village republic
spotlights.spot_it: A village council of elders that owns the land, runs the forest, settles disputes and decides who may hunt.
spotlights.story_md: Each Naga village was, in effect, its own small state, with its own council, its own land and its own law. That survives. Under Article 371A, Naga customary law and the ownership of land are protected, so most land belongs to villages, clans and families, not the government. Village councils settle many disputes, from land to marriage, under customary law. They can also act fast: Khonoma's council created a 20 square km sanctuary in 1998, and Pangti's patrols ended falcon hunting. In 2002 the state began communitisation, handing village schools, health centres and power lines to community boards. The flip side is that customary bodies are almost all male.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Real power in Nagaland often sits with the village, not the state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every village a republic, every council a court.

spotlights.name: The first women in the assembly, 2023
spotlights.spot_it: Two women among 60 MLAs: Hekani Jakhalu for Dimapur III and Salhoutuonuo Kruse for Western Angami.
spotlights.story_md: Nagaland had been a state for 60 years before a single woman won a seat in its assembly. In the 2023 election Hekani Jakhalu, a lawyer who founded the youth organisation YouthNet and had received the Nari Shakti Puraskar, won Dimapur III, and Salhoutuonuo Kruse won Western Angami. Kruse became the state's first woman minister. Before them the state's only woman in the Lok Sabha had been Rano Shaiza in 1977. Women in Nagaland are highly visible in church, business and education, but many tribal bodies argued that reserved seats for women in town councils broke customary law, and the issue sparked violent protests in 2017. Elections with women's reservation were finally held in 2024.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A test of how customary law and equal rights fit together.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sixty years, then two women at once.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Nagaland is small, so a few people loom large. The national movement produced Phizo, the Naga Club and the NSCN leaders Isak Chishi Swu and Thuingaleng Muivah. Freedom fighters on India's side included Rani Gaidinliu. The church produced pastors and translators whose names every Naga Baptist knows.

Modern Nagaland has produced doctors, athletes, writers and musicians who are known well beyond the state. Below are three: a barefoot football captain, a novelist who writes in English about Angami villages and spirits, and the politician who has led the state for most of the 21st century.

spotlights.name: Talimeren Ao
spotlights.spot_it: India's first football captain at an Olympics, who played barefoot at Wembley in 1948.
spotlights.story_md: Talimeren Ao captained India at the 1948 London Olympics, the country's first Olympic football match after independence, and carried the Indian flag at the opening ceremony. India lost 2-1 to France, and most of the Indian team played without boots, in thick socks and bandages. When the press asked about it, he is reported to have said that in India we play football, while you play bootball. He played centre-half for Mohun Bagan from 1943 and captained the club. He also qualified as a doctor at R. G. Kar Medical College in Kolkata and became Director of Health Services in Nagaland, retiring in 1978. India Post issued a stamp in his honour in 2018.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He represented a new India while the Naga question was still unresolved.
spotlights.memory_hook: Barefoot at Wembley: we play football, you play bootball.

spotlights.name: Easterine Kire

where.label: Born Kohima; lives in northern Norway

spotlights.spot_it: The Angami writer who put Naga village life into English novels and poems.
spotlights.story_md: Easterine Kire was born in Kohima in 1959 into an Angami family. Her poetry collection Kelhoukevira, from 1982, is described as the first book of Naga poetry published in English, and A Naga Village Remembered, from 2003, as the first Naga novel in English. It retells the story of Khonoma's war with the British. Her novel When the River Sleeps, about a hunter seeking a magical stone, won The Hindu Literary Prize in 2015, and Spirit Nights won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 2024. She writes about spirits, war, women and memory, and lives in northern Norway, where she also performs jazz poetry. Her books are among the best ways into Naga life for outsiders.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She gave Naga oral history a home in world literature.
spotlights.memory_hook: Khonoma's war, told by its own great-granddaughter.

spotlights.name: Neiphiu Rio
spotlights.spot_it: The longest-serving Chief Minister of Nagaland, usually in a red Naga shawl.
spotlights.story_md: Neiphiu Rio, born in Tuophema in 1950, is the longest-serving Chief Minister of Nagaland. He has led the state from 2003 to 2008, from 2008 to 2014 and again since March 2018, with a spell in the Lok Sabha in between. He started in the Congress, joined the Naga People's Front in 2002, moved to the new NDPP in 2018, and in October 2025 merged the NDPP into the NPF, becoming NPF president on 21 October 2025. That leaves almost the whole assembly in or allied with his party, and the opposition thin. His nephew Theja Rio is the filmmaker who won at Toronto in 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: For a generation, Nagaland's government has had one face.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four parties, one man, nearly two decades in charge.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Almost every visitor arrives at Dimapur, by train or plane, and drives about 70 km up into the hills to Kohima. From there the classic trips are a day at Kohima's war cemetery, cathedral and Kohima village; the walk to Dzükou Valley from Viswema or Jakhama; a night in Khonoma; and, in December, the Hornbill Festival at Kisama.

Further afield, Mokokchung is the heart of Ao country and a cultural capital in its own right. Wokha has the Doyang reservoir and the falcons of Pangti, best in late October and early November. Mon and Longwa, in the far north-east, are the land of the Konyak and the Anghs, and best during Aoleang in April. Kiphire leads toward Saramati. Roads are slow, so give each trip more time than the map suggests. Indian visitors need an Inner Line Permit, which can be applied for online.

spotlights.name: Kohima
spotlights.when: Capital; founded as a British post in 1878
spotlights.spot_it: A ridge town of houses stacked on steep slopes, under Mount Japfü, with a war cemetery at its centre.
spotlights.story_md: Kohima began as an Angami village, Kohima village or Bara Basti, which still sits on its own hill. The British set up their district headquarters beside it in 1878, and the town grew around the road to Imphal. In 1944 the battle smashed much of it. Today it is the capital, at about 1,450 m, a dense town of concrete and tin roofs built along ridges, with traffic that crawls along the single main road. Its landmarks are the war cemetery, the Catholic cathedral, the state museum, the Capital Cultural Centre and Kohima village itself. It is the base for Dzükou, Khonoma and the Hornbill Festival at Kisama, 12 km away.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The capital holds the state's war, faith and politics on one ridge.
spotlights.memory_hook: A town built on a battlefield, with a village older than both.

spotlights.name: Longwa

where.label: Mon district, on the Myanmar border

spotlights.spot_it: A Konyak hilltop village where the chief's house is cut in two by the international border.
spotlights.story_md: Longwa is a Konyak village in Mon district that straddles the border with Myanmar. The line runs straight through the house of the Angh, the hereditary chief, so he is said to eat in one country and sleep in another. His authority covers the whole village and, by tradition, dozens of Konyak villages on both sides of the border and into Arunachal Pradesh. The 2011 census counted 6,703 people. Many villagers have relatives and fields across the line, and a road runs on to Loji in Myanmar. India ended free movement across this border in 2024 and plans to fence it, which matters here more than almost anywhere: for Longwa, the border is not an edge but a hallway.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how artificial the India-Myanmar border is for the Nagas.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dinner in India, bedtime in Myanmar.

spotlights.name: Dimapur
spotlights.when: Largest city; only airport and main railhead
spotlights.spot_it: A flat, hot, busy trading town on the plains edge, with the only airport and the railway.
spotlights.story_md: Dimapur is the one big place in Nagaland that is not in the hills. It sits on the plain beside Assam, at about 150 m, and it is the state's commercial city, transport hub and the place where tribes, plainspeople and migrants mix most. Its twin with Chümoukedima is the largest urban area in the state. Nagaland's only airport is 7 km away, with flights to Kolkata, Guwahati and elsewhere, and the main railway station is here, so almost every visitor arrives through Dimapur and then drives about 70 km up to Kohima. The old Kachari capital stood here. Nagamese is the native language of some Dimasa families in the town, the only place where it is a mother tongue.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without Dimapur, the hill state would have no front door.
spotlights.memory_hook: Arrive in the plains, climb to the capital.

sections.title: How it earns
sections.intro_md:
Nagaland's economy is small and leans on Delhi. The state budget for 2026-27 expects **₹48,500 crore** of output, about ₹1.92 lakh per person in 2025-26, below India's average. More than 60% of people depend on farming, much of it jhum, with rice the main crop and pineapple, ginger, king chilli, oranges and tea in pockets.

The government is the biggest employer. In the 2026-27 budget, **86%** of the state's revenue comes from the Centre as tax shares and grants, and own taxes are only about 4.3% of GSDP. Salaries, pensions and interest eat 68% of revenue receipts, leaving little for roads and schools. Private industry is thin, held back by poor roads, insurgency-era taxes collected by armed groups, and land that is owned by communities rather than sold. Tourism, built around Hornbill, Dzükou and the Konyak, and the digital and services work of young Nagas in Indian cities are the growth stories.

spotlights.name: Jhum, slash-and-burn farming
spotlights.spot_it: Patchwork hillsides: brown cleared plots, green crops and grey-green regrowth at different ages, side by side.
spotlights.story_md: Most Nagas still live from the land, and much of that land is farmed by jhum. A family or clan clears a patch of forest in winter, burns the slash in March, and sows rice mixed with maize, millets, beans, chillies, gourds and taro in the ash. After one or two years the plot is left to regrow, and the farmer moves on, returning years later. With long fallows it can be sustainable; as population grows and fallows shrink, it erodes soil and forests. Villages decide which slopes to clear each year, which is why the jhum calendar sets the festival calendar. Wet terraces, like those of the Angami and Chakhesang, are the main alternative.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shapes the landscape, the diet and the festivals.
spotlights.memory_hook: Burn in March, sow in ash, move on.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
Nagaland suffers from stereotypes, many from people who have never been there. Some are old fears from the insurgency years; some are about food; some come from photographs of tattooed headhunters. Here are the common ones, checked against evidence.

The pattern behind most of them is the same: a real fact from one time, place or tribe is stretched to cover all Nagas at all times. Headhunting was real, but it ended generations ago. The insurgency was real, but a ceasefire has held since 1997.

data.evidence: Headhunting ended in the 20th century; the last tattooed Konyak headhunters are now very old men.
The origin of the word is uncertain; one Assamese explanation is people with pierced ears.
Some do; pork is the everyday meat. A 2020 ban was struck down in 2023.
A ceasefire with the main armed group has held since 1997.
The Total Prohibition Act of 1989 is still in force, though widely flouted.
Each people has its own; Nagamese and English bridge them.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
Politics reshuffled in October 2025, when Chief Minister Neiphiu Rio merged his NDPP into the Naga People's Front, the party he had left in 2017, and became its president on 21 October 2025. The Election Commission recognised the merger in May 2026. The Naga peace talks remain unfinished more than a decade after the 2015 Framework Agreement.

On the border, India's decision in February 2024 to end free movement across the Myanmar border and to fence it remains a live grievance in Mon, Noklak and the east. On the Assam boundary, the two states said on 23 October 2026 that they had jointly decided on evictions along the inter-state border. Dzükou burned again in January 2026. In culture, Theja Rio's film Angh won the Platform Prize at Toronto in September 2026, and in October 2026 Lanuakum Longkumer of Nagaland finished the World's Highest Marathon. The 2026 Hornbill Festival runs from 1 to 10 December.

spotlights.name: Angh, the film that won at Toronto
spotlights.spot_it: A film by Nagaland's Theja Rio that won the Platform Prize at TIFF 2026.
spotlights.story_md: At the Toronto International Film Festival, held from 10 to 20 September 2026, the Platform Prize went to Angh, directed by Theja Rio from Nagaland. Platform is TIFF's juried section for directors with a distinct voice, so the award put a Naga filmmaker in the same conversation as international art-house cinema. The title is the Konyak word for a hereditary chief, the same office that the Angh of Longwa holds. Detailed descriptions of the film's story and language were not available in the sources checked for this day. Theja Rio is the nephew of Chief Minister Neiphiu Rio. The win followed years of growth in Naga short film and documentary.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A sign that Naga stories are reaching world screens on their own terms.
spotlights.memory_hook: A chief's title, on a Toronto stage.

spotlights.name: The end of free movement across the Myanmar border

where.label: India-Myanmar border, Mon, Noklak, Kiphire, Phek

spotlights.spot_it: A plan to fence 1,643 km of border that cuts through Naga villages, clans and fields.
spotlights.story_md: For decades, people living near the India-Myanmar border could cross up to 16 km without a visa, an arrangement called the Free Movement Regime. In February 2024, after ethnic violence in Manipur and concern about smuggling and armed groups, India ended it and announced a fence along the 1,643 km border, with about ₹30,000 crore approved. By September 2024 only about 30 km had been fenced, and work is expected to take until 2035-36. In Nagaland, Naga bodies, churches and the state government have opposed the fence because it would split Naga villages and families that straddle the line, like Longwa. The fence is, for many Nagas, the old partition made concrete.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It may decide whether the Naga homeland stays one place in daily life.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fence through a chief's house.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
Nagaland is a small hill state on the Myanmar border: about 20 lakh people in 17 major peoples, joined by Nagamese, English and the church. Once a land of self-governing hilltop villages that took heads, it was the last frontier the British tamed and the place where Japan's invasion of India stopped on a tennis court in 1944. It fought India for independence, won statehood in 1963 and a constitution that protects its land and customs, and still waits for a final peace. It became the most Baptist place on earth in a century. Its food runs on smoke, ferment and the king chilli; its year on festivals from Sekrenyi to Hornbill.

Tomorrow you will forget most of this. Do today's cards and the quiz, and some of it will stay.

side_dish.title: Why chilli burns: capsaicin and the Scoville scale
side_dish.body_md:
The Naga king chilli does not actually burn you. It tricks you. Its heat comes from **capsaicin**, a molecule the plant makes in the pale ribs inside the fruit. Capsaicin fits into a receptor on your nerve endings called **TRPV1**, whose real job is to warn you of temperatures above about 43°C. When capsaicin docks there, the nerve fires exactly as if your mouth were being scalded, so your brain sends sweat, tears, a red face and a racing pulse. No tissue is damaged.

Why would a plant do this? Mammals, which chew and destroy seeds, feel the burn. Birds, which swallow chilli seeds whole and spread them, have a version of TRPV1 that capsaicin does not trigger. A chilli is hot for us and mild for a bulbul.

In 1912 a pharmacist named Wilbur Scoville measured heat by diluting a chilli extract in sugar water until a panel of tasters could no longer feel it. A bell pepper scores 0. Tabasco scores about 2,500 to 5,000. The Naga king chilli scores about a million: its extract has to be diluted about a million times before the heat disappears. Labs now measure capsaicin directly with chromatography and convert the result to Scoville units.

Water spreads capsaicin around, because it does not dissolve in water. Fat and protein, such as milk or yoghurt, carry it away. Nagas, whose cooking uses little dairy, eat their chilli with heaps of plain rice instead.

offline_task.title: Make a Naga-style roasted tomato and chilli chutney
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 4 as a side. About 20 minutes.** This is the everyday chutney on Naga tables: smoky, sharp and hot. Use a milder chilli unless you know what you are doing.

**You need**
- 4 ripe tomatoes
- 2 to 4 green or red chillies (or 1 small piece of dried king chilli, if you can get it, handled with gloves)
- 4 cloves garlic, unpeeled
- A thumb of ginger
- A handful of fresh coriander
- Salt

**Steps**
1. Roast the tomatoes, chillies and garlic directly over a gas flame or under a grill, turning, until the skins are black in patches and the tomatoes are soft. This is the smoke that gives the chutney its Naga taste.
2. Let them cool a little, then peel the garlic and pull off the loosest burnt tomato skin. Leave some char.
3. In a mortar, or a bowl with the back of a spoon, pound the garlic, ginger and chillies with a pinch of salt to a paste.
4. Add the tomatoes and mash roughly. It should be chunky, not smooth.
5. Stir in chopped coriander and taste for salt.
6. Eat with plain rice and boiled greens or any simple meat.

**Notice**: there is no oil and no cooked spice in it. Naga flavour comes from smoke, sourness and chilli, not from a tadka.

best_facts.fact: The Japanese advance into India in 1944 was fought to a halt across a tennis court in Kohima. Its lines are still painted white in concrete, inside the war cemetery.
best_facts.why_surprising: A garden court decided a world war front.

best_facts.fact: In the Konyak village of Longwa, the India-Myanmar border runs through the chief's house: he is said to eat in one country and sleep in the other.
In 2012 an estimated 12,000 to 14,000 Amur falcons a day were being trapped at Doyang. By 2013 the killing there had stopped, and Pangti now calls itself the falcon capital of the world.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of the fastest conservation turnarounds anywhere.

best_facts.fact: Nagaland went from zero Christians in 1871 to about 88% Christian, mostly Baptist, and is called the only predominantly Baptist state in the world.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Baptist heartland in the Himalayan foothills.

best_facts.fact: Most of the cost of Kohima's Catholic cathedral was paid by Japanese donors, as a memorial to the Japanese soldiers who died attacking Kohima.
best_facts.why_surprising: The losers of the battle built its church.

best_facts.fact: Phizo declared Naga independence on 14 August 1947, a day before India's own, and died 43 years later in a London suburb, never allowed home alive.
best_facts.why_surprising: Independence day came early, and exile lasted 30 years.

best_facts.fact: Nagaland was the only Indian state whose population fell between 2001 and 2011.
Talimeren Ao captained India barefoot at the 1948 Olympics and reportedly said: in India we play football, you play bootball. He later became a doctor and ran Nagaland's health services.
best_facts.why_surprising: A footballer, a flag-bearer and a physician.

best_facts.fact: The Naga king chilli was certified by Guinness as the hottest in the world in 2007, at about a million Scoville units, and farmers smear it on fences to keep elephants away.
best_facts.why_surprising: A chilli that doubles as an elephant fence.

best_facts.fact: In 1998 hunters from Khonoma killed about 300 Blyth's tragopans in a single contest; the shock led the village to ban hunting over 20 square km, and in 2005 it was called India's first green village.
best_facts.why_surprising: A massacre turned a village into conservationists.

best_facts.fact: Konyak brass pendants are cast as rows of tiny human heads; each face recorded an enemy head taken in a raid.
Nagaland's two first women MLAs were elected in 2023, sixty years after statehood.
The Naga peoples speak dozens of languages, so the state's real common tongue is Nagamese, a creole of Assamese born in barter markets, while English is the official language.
best_facts.why_surprising: A state united by a market language.

best_facts.fact: Axone, fermented soybean, smells so strong that a 2019 film, Axone, is built around northeastern friends in Delhi trying to cook it without upsetting the neighbours.
best_facts.why_surprising: A smell with its own movie.

best_facts.fact: The Kohima Epitaph, read at Remembrance services worldwide, was probably modelled on the Greek epitaph for the Spartans at Thermopylae.
best_facts.why_surprising: Ancient Greece in a Naga hill cemetery.

best_facts.fact: Under Article 371A no Act of Parliament on Naga customs or land applies in Nagaland unless the state assembly agrees, so most land belongs to villages and clans, not the state.
In 2026-27, about 86% of Nagaland's state revenue comes from the Centre.
best_facts.why_surprising: A state that runs on transfers.
